newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Amstrad slides back into loss.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Amstrad slides back into loss.

text.p: Amstrad Plc slipped back into the red last year, but the British electronics group that was once a stock market darling said on Tuesday that rationalisation of its consumer electronics business would help stem its losses.
The group made a loss before tax of 14.9 million pounds ($23.15 million) in the year to June 30 after a profit of 3.1 million last time. Sales rose to 329.3 million pounds from 271.6 million.
A fundamental shake up of Amstrad Consumer Electronics, (ACE), originally the mainstay of the company, cost 10.7 million pounds in restructuring and redundancy costs.
Chairman and founder Alan Sugar said the rationalisation was a major change in the focus of the group, which became a high flier in the 1980s by selling personal computers to ordinary people.

The success of the Amstrad PC turned the group into a stock market favourite, with a valuation of about one billion pounds, before its products started losing ground to competitors from the United States and Japan.
Sugar said the group would now concentrate on building up its technology-based businesses -- Dancall, Viglen and Dataflex Design Communications.
"ACE's losses which have been a drain on the group for so long should not reoccur," he said in a statement.
Amstrad tried to reorganised ACE earlier this year, but deteriorating trading conditions in Europe meant the surgery was not radical enough.
ACE's activities in audio, video, television and facsimile products have been taken on by Betacom Plc, a company majority-owned by Amstrad.
Betacom will sell from ACE's stocks until they run out and then sell Amstrad branded products directly from suppliers.
Sugar said the arrangement with Betacom would mean significant cost reductions via job cuts which were expected to eliminate loss-making activities.
Amstrad expressed regret that a possible takeover by Psion Plc earlier this year was called off because of failure to agree merger terms.
Psion, a leading producer of hand-held personal oganisers, said on June 25 it was holding talks with Amstrad on a possible bid. But the deal was czlled off by July 26.
"Unfortunately, the discussions were terminated because we were unable to reach agreement on the terms of a merger," said Sugar, who still owns around a third of the company.
He also chairs Tottenham Hotspur Plc, the English Premier League soccer club.
Amstrad's mobile phone business Dancall also had a tough year. Competitive market conditions put pressure on prices and margins which resulted in losses in the second half.
Amstrad warned in May that weakness in the market of the Danish-based company meant that its initial contribution to group profits was unlikely until the next financial year.
Amstrad's shares rose in morning trading by 10 pence to 148.5 pence. ($1=.6436 Pound)
